faq.q: When is a brain biopsy required?

faq.a: It increases risk of primary CNS lymphoma and may alter chemotherapy tolerance.

exam: A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with seizures and a solitary ring‑enhancing lesion on CT – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Consider CSF cytology and MRI if possible; differentiate lymphoma from toxoplasmosis.

A child with cerebellar tumour shows truncal ataxia and hydrocephalus – which emergency measure should be taken first? — Administer dexamethasone to reduce oedema and arrange urgent neurosurgical referral.
Explain why temozolomide is preferred over nitrosoureas in low‑resource settings for glioblastoma. — Oral administration, lower myelosuppression, no need for infusion equipment.

A patient on long‑term steroids develops fever and cough – what complication must you suspect and how would you manage it? — Opportunistic infection (TB or fungal); stop steroids if possible, start appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
How does WHO grade influence prognosis and treatment planning? — Higher grade (III‑IV) predicts rapid progression; mandates aggressive multimodal therapy.
What are red‑flag signs on neuro‑exam that mandate urgent imaging? — New papilledema, unilateral cranial nerve palsy, rapidly evolving motor weakness.

Distinguish primary CNS lymphoma from high‑grade glioma on imaging and clinical clues. — Lymphoma often in immunocompromised, homogeneous enhancement, deep periventricular location; glioma shows heterogeneous necrosis.
Why is prophylactic antiepileptic therapy not recommended for all brain tumour patients? — Only indicated after a seizure; routine use increases side‑effects without proven benefit.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Neuro‑oncology deals with primary and secondary tumours of the brain and spinal cord, focusing on diagnosis, staging, and management in low‑resource settings. It integrates clinical reasoning, limited investigations, and pragmatic treatment choices.

b: Incidence peaks in children (medulloblastoma) and older adults (glioblastoma).
Metastases often arise from lung, breast, or melanoma.
sections.p: Primary CNS tumours (gliomas, medulloblastoma, meningioma) and metastatic lesions are common causes of focal neurological deficits. In East Africa, HIV‑related primary CNS lymphoma and TB meningitis mimics are frequent.

b: WHO grade correlates with aggressiveness; grade IV = glioblastoma, poorest prognosis.
RPA groups consider age, Karnofsky performance status, and tumour control.
sections.p: Diagnosis rests on pattern of symptoms, neuro‑exam localisation, and imaging when available. Staging uses WHO grade (I‑IV) for primary tumours and the RPA classification for metastases.

b: Seizure at onset → consider low‑grade glioma or metastasis.
Progressive focal deficit → localisation helps narrow tumour type.
sections.p: Patients present with headache, seizures, focal weakness, or signs of raised intracranial pressure. Early recognition prevents irreversible deficits and guides urgent referral.

t.b: Detects mass effect, hydrocephalus, calcifications; confirms tumour presence when MRI unavailable.
Defines tumour margins, oedema, and distinguishes tumour from abscess; preferred if accessible.
Answers if leptomeningeal spread is present; positive cells indicate metastatic or lymphoma spread.
Identifies HIV‑related primary CNS lymphoma, which alters management.
Assesses baseline for surgery/chemotherapy and detects anemia or coagulopathy.

b: Corticosteroids (dexamethasone) for symptomatic oedema; avoid long‑term high dose due to infection risk.
Surgical excision when tumour is accessible and patient’s performance status >70.
Temozolomide oral chemotherapy for glioblastoma if radiotherapy unavailable; chosen for oral route and modest toxicity.
Radiotherapy (30 Gy in 10 fractions) for palliation when full course not feasible.
Supportive care: antiepileptics for seizures, physiotherapy, psychosocial support.
sections.p: Treatment combines surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, adapted to resources. Goal is maximal safe resection, control oedema, and palliation.

Unilateral papilledema + focal deficit → mass lesion on that side.
Seizure with no prior epilepsy → consider tumour, especially if focal.
sections.p: Focus on localisation, red‑flag signs, and pragmatic work‑up.

Delaying steroids in acute ICP; can worsen herniation.
